title: Crawlspace Moisture: The Silent Threat to Georgia Foundations
description: Crawlspace moisture is a major risk in Metro Atlanta. Learn the signs of wood rot and foundation damage from Certified Master Inspector Christopher Boykin.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI

content:
In Metro Atlanta and across Georgia, many homes are built over a crawlspace rather than a basement or slab. Crawlspaces are incredibly common, but they also host one of the most frequent findings we uncover during home inspections: crawlspace moisture. Because of our highly humid summers and clay soils, moisture in crawlspaces is a silent threat that can damage structural integrity and diminish indoor air quality.

At Foresight Home Inspections, we send two certified inspectors on every single property audit. One of our primary tasks is to crawl directly into these tight spaces, equipped with FLIR thermal imaging cameras and digital moisture meters, to see what is happening beneath your feet. We don't just stand at the access door—we scan every corner of the floor framing to make sure your home is fully protected.

Why Crawlspace Moisture is a Major Risk in Georgia

Crawlspaces naturally accumulate humidity because they are situated directly over the bare soil. In North Georgia, heavy summer rains soak the clay around foundations, and this moisture slowly evaporates into the crawlspace air. When that warm, damp air contacts cooler floor joists or AC ducts, it condenses into water droplets.

If wood joists are exposed to this water for long periods, they begin to decay. Over time, this leads to structural sagging, spongy floors, and the growth of active mold spores. What this could mean is that your subfloor is rotting, your family is breathing mold spores through floor vents, or your foundation structure is losing its load-bearing capacity. Our recommendation in these situations is: have a licensed structural or moisture mitigation contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

Common Signs of a Wet Crawlspace You Can Spot

While you might not want to crawl under your house yourself, there are several warning signs you can easily spot from inside your living spaces:

  • Musty Odors — A persistent, damp smell in the home, particularly near baseboards and closets, is a classic sign of crawlspace mold.
  • Cupping Wood Floors — When crawlspace humidity is high, the bottom of hardwood flooring absorbs moisture and expands, causing the edges of the boards to cup or warp upward.
  • Sagging or Soft Spots — If walking across your living room feels slightly bouncy or uneven, the floor framing below may have lost strength due to rot.
  • High Indoor Humidity — Up to 50% of the air on the first floor of a home originates in the crawlspace due to the "stack effect." A wet crawlspace directly raises humidity throughout the house.

How to Solve Crawlspace Moisture Concerns

Fixing crawlspace moisture depends on how severe the water intrusion is. For minor humidity, installing a thick 6-mil or 10-mil vapor barrier over the bare soil is highly effective. The plastic barrier blocks ground moisture from rising into the air and keeps floor joists dry.

For more active leaks, a combination of a sump pump, perimeter french drains, or a crawlspace dehumidifier might be required. In extreme cases, full crawlspace encapsulation—where the space is completely sealed, insulated, and conditioned—is the gold standard. If we find excessive standing water or falling insulation under your house, our recommendation is: have a licensed crawlspace encapsulation contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

That is why we offer dedicated Short-Term Rental (STR) Compliance Assist services. We send a dual-inspector team to perform standardized, third-party safety audits starting at our highly competitive base rates, ensuring your listing remains fully compliant and online without interruptions.

The Rising Wave of STR Regulations in Metro Atlanta

Municipalities across Georgia are cracking down on unregistered short-term rentals. For instance, cities like Atlanta, Sandy Springs, Decatur, and Marietta, as well as counties like Cobb and DeKalb, have established strict safety inspection protocols. To qualify for an STR license, hosts must submit proof of a certified third-party safety inspection.

These local ordinances are designed to protect guests, but a single failed item can delay your permit for weeks, costing you valuable booking revenue. What this could mean is that you could face heavy local fines, listing suspension on Airbnb and Vrbo, or outright denial of your business license. Our recommendation is: have a licensed third-party inspector perform a pre-compliance safety audit and repair any noted defects as needed.

What a Short-Term Rental Safety Audit Covers

During an STR compliance inspection, our inspectors check a comprehensive list of health and safety items required by most Georgia local governments. Some of the most critical checklist items include:

  • Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors — Must be installed in every bedroom, on every level of the home, and tested to ensure they are fully operational and not expired.
  • Emergency Egress — Every sleeping room must feature a primary window or door that opens easily from the inside without keys or special tools, providing a safe escape route.
  • Electrical Panel and Outlet Safety — All outlets in kitchens, bathrooms, and wet bars must be GFCI-protected, and the main breaker panel must be clear of any fire hazards or double-taps.
  • Fire Extinguishers — A fully charged, multi-purpose fire extinguisher (typically 2A:10BC rated) must be mounted in a highly visible location, such as the kitchen, with active certification tags.
  • Structural & Deck Safety — Railings on stairs and balconies must be secure, and spindles must be spaced close enough to prevent falls, meeting local structural safety standards.

By sending two certified inspectors, we can perform a highly efficient inspection of your property. We provide a detailed digital report with high-resolution photos and video within 24 hours that you can submit directly to county licensing portals.

Our STR safety audits start at our standard flat base rate of $355+ based on the size of your property. Additionally, because Christopher Boykin is a Certified Master Inspector, every safety audit includes our standard elite InterNACHI-backed standards. We cover your major mechanicals (HVAC, plumbing, electrical) and structural framing, giving you and your guests absolute peace of mind.

What Factors Affect Home Inspection Cost?

Several key variables influence the final cost of a home inspection in the Metro Atlanta area. Understanding these factors helps you anticipate your total investment and avoid unexpected charges.

Square Footage

The single largest factor in home inspection pricing is the total square footage of the property. Larger homes require more time to inspect. A 4,000 square foot home in Alpharetta has significantly more roof area, more plumbing fixtures, additional HVAC systems, and more electrical circuits than a 1,200 square foot condo in Midtown. Our pricing tiers reflect this reality, ensuring you pay a fair price based on the actual scope of work.

Property Age

Older homes in established Atlanta neighborhoods like Decatur, Grant Park, East Lake, and Kirkwood often have aging systems that require more detailed evaluation. Homes built before 1980 may have outdated electrical panels (such as Federal Pacific or Zinsco), galvanized steel plumbing, original single-pane windows, and older HVAC equipment. While the base inspection fee covers a thorough evaluation regardless of age, older properties sometimes benefit from add-on services like sewer scope inspections to check aging underground pipes.

Foundation Type

Georgia homes are built on three primary foundation types: slab-on-grade, crawlspace, and full basement. Properties with crawlspaces require our inspectors to physically enter and inspect the sub-floor environment, checking floor joists, vapor barriers, insulation, and foundation piers. Homes with basements require evaluation of basement walls, sump pumps, and potential water intrusion points. Each foundation type demands different inspection time and techniques.

Crawlspace Access and Condition

Crawlspace inspections can vary significantly. A well-maintained, encapsulated crawlspace with adequate clearance is straightforward. However, a low-clearance, un-encapsulated crawlspace with standing water, limited access points, or excessive debris requires more time and effort. In Metro Atlanta, our humid climate frequently creates challenging crawlspace conditions that demand thorough moisture evaluation.

Number of Systems

Homes with multiple HVAC systems, multiple water heaters, detached garages, guest houses, or finished basements with separate mechanical zones naturally require additional inspection time. Our pricing ensures comprehensive coverage regardless of system count.

Add-On Services and Their Costs

Radon Testing: $175 to $200

Radon is an invisible, odorless radioactive gas that seeps through foundation cracks and is the second leading cause of lung cancer. We deploy continuous 48-hour professional diagnostic monitors that capture hourly readings, providing far more accurate results than passive mail-in kits. The EPA has identified elevated radon levels in homes across Fulton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Cobb, Cherokee, and Forsyth counties. Read more about the hidden dangers of radon in Georgia homes.

Termite and Wood Destroying Organism (WDO) Inspection: $100 to $175

Georgia's warm, humid climate makes it a prime environment for subterranean and Formosan termites. A dedicated WDO inspection produces the Official Georgia Wood Infestation Report required by most mortgage lenders for closing. This is separate from the structural home inspection and examines crawlspaces, sill plates, and exterior foundations for active insect activity and conducive conditions. Learn more in our guide to termites and wood destroying organisms.

Sewer Scope Inspection: $425

A sewer scope uses a high-definition camera to inspect the buried lateral sewer line running from your home to the municipal connection. We identify root intrusions, pipe collapses, bellies, offsets, and corrosion that can lead to catastrophic sewage backups costing $5,000 to $15,000 in excavation and repair. This service is especially recommended for homes older than 20 years. Check out our complete sewer scope inspection guide for details.

Pool and Spa Inspection: $300

A standard home inspection does not cover swimming pools or spas. Our dedicated pool inspection evaluates the structural shell, mechanical equipment (pumps, filters, heaters), electrical safety, plumbing lines, safety compliance (fencing, gates, drain covers), and overall condition. Pool repairs are notoriously expensive, and this $300 investment regularly saves buyers thousands. Read our pool and spa inspection guide to learn more.

title: What Fails a Home Inspection? Top 10 Deal Breakers in Georgia
description: Learn the top 10 issues that fail a home inspection in Georgia, from roof damage and foundation cracks to electrical hazards and mold. Certified Master Inspector Christopher Boykin explains what deal breakers to watch for and what to do if problems are found.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
keywords: things that fail a home inspection
content:
Key Takeaway: A home inspection does not technically "pass" or "fail" a property. However, certain major defects — such as structural foundation damage, active roof leaks, hazardous electrical wiring, and environmental dangers like radon — are commonly considered deal breakers that can derail a real estate transaction. Knowing what to look for helps you negotiate effectively and protect your investment.

One of the most common questions homebuyers ask us is: what fails a home inspection? It is important to understand that a professional home inspection is not a pass-or-fail test. There is no official score or grade. Instead, a home inspection is a comprehensive evaluation of the property's current condition, systems, and safety. That said, there are certain findings so significant that they can — and often do — stop a real estate deal in its tracks.

As a Certified Master Inspector serving 163+ cities across Metro Atlanta, Christopher Boykin and the two-inspector team at Foresight Home Inspections have evaluated thousands of properties. In this guide, we share the top 10 deal breakers we encounter most frequently in Georgia homes, along with expert advice on what to do when these issues are discovered.

1. Roof Damage and Active Leaks

The roof is the home's primary defense against Georgia's intense summer storms, heavy rainfall, and occasional hail. Roof damage is consistently one of the most impactful findings in any home inspection because the repair costs are substantial and the consequences of ignoring it are severe.

Common roof issues we identify include:

  • Missing, cracked, or curling shingles indicating end-of-life deterioration
  • Damaged or improperly installed flashing around chimneys, skylights, and valleys
  • Active water stains on the underside of roof decking visible from the attic
  • Sagging or soft spots in the roof structure indicating potential rot
  • Granule loss on asphalt shingles (a sign of significant weathering)

What this could mean: A failing roof can lead to water intrusion throughout the entire structure, causing mold growth, wood rot, damaged insulation, and ruined ceilings and walls. A full roof replacement in Metro Atlanta costs between $8,000 and $25,000 depending on size and materials. Our recommendation is: have a licensed roofing contractor evaluate further and provide a repair or replacement estimate.

2. Foundation Cracks and Structural Movement

Georgia's notorious red clay soils expand when wet and contract when dry, creating constant pressure on home foundations. Foundation problems are among the most expensive defects to repair and are a leading cause of deal cancellations.

Warning signs include:

  • Horizontal or diagonal cracks in basement or crawlspace foundation walls
  • Stair-step cracking in exterior brick mortar joints
  • Doors and windows that stick, jam, or will not close properly
  • Visible floor slope or unevenness when walking through the home
  • Gaps between walls and ceilings or walls and floors

What this could mean: Active foundation settlement can compromise the entire structural integrity of the home. Repair costs using steel piers, helical anchors, or carbon fiber wall supports range from $5,000 to $30,000 depending on severity. Our recommendation is: have a licensed structural engineer or foundation contractor evaluate further and repair as needed. Read our detailed foundation inspection guide for more information.

3. Electrical Hazards

Electrical defects are among the most dangerous findings in a home inspection because they present immediate fire and electrocution risks. In Metro Atlanta, we regularly encounter electrical hazards in homes of all ages.

Critical electrical issues include:

  • Federal Pacific or Zinsco electrical panels — These outdated panels are known for failing to trip during overloads, creating serious fire hazards. Replacement is strongly recommended.
  • Double-tapped breakers — Two wires connected to a single breaker terminal creates loose connections and potential arcing.
  • Ungrounded outlets — Two-prong outlets without proper grounding pose shock risks, especially in older homes.
  • Missing GFCI protection — Kitchens, bathrooms, garages, and exterior outlets require Ground Fault Circuit Interrupter protection to prevent electrocution in wet areas.
  • Exposed or damaged wiring — DIY electrical work, improperly secured junction boxes, and deteriorated wiring insulation are common hazards.

What this could mean: Electrical hazards present immediate safety risks including house fires and electrocution. An electrical panel replacement costs $1,500 to $4,000, while whole-house rewiring can exceed $10,000. Our recommendation is: have a licensed electrical contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

4. Plumbing Problems

Plumbing defects range from minor inconveniences to catastrophic failures. In Georgia, the variety of pipe materials used across different construction eras creates unique challenges for inspectors and buyers alike.

Significant plumbing concerns include:

  • Active leaks at supply lines, drain connections, or fixture valves
  • Galvanized steel supply pipes (common in pre-1970s homes) showing heavy corrosion and reduced water pressure
  • Polybutylene (poly-b) piping, a defective material prone to sudden failure that was widely installed in Georgia homes from the late 1970s through the mid-1990s
  • Water heaters with rusted tanks, missing safety features, or expired lifespans
  • Sewage odors indicating broken drain lines or failed wax seals

What this could mean: A burst supply line or failed main drain can cause tens of thousands of dollars in water damage to flooring, drywall, and personal property. A whole-house repipe costs $5,000 to $15,000. Our recommendation is: have a licensed plumbing contractor evaluate further and repair as needed. We also recommend adding a sewer scope inspection to check buried drain lines.

5. HVAC System Failure

In Georgia, your heating and air conditioning system is not a luxury — it is a necessity for survival during our intense summers when temperatures regularly exceed 95 degrees. HVAC defects can render a home uncomfortable and expensive to operate.

Common HVAC failures include:

  • Systems that fail to cool or heat to within normal temperature differentials
  • Cracked heat exchangers in gas furnaces (a carbon monoxide hazard)
  • Refrigerant leaks and failing compressors
  • Disconnected, crushed, or poorly sealed ductwork in attics and crawlspaces
  • Units that have exceeded their expected useful life (typically 15 to 20 years)

What this could mean: Replacing a central HVAC system in Metro Atlanta costs $6,000 to $15,000 per unit. A cracked heat exchanger is a serious safety hazard that requires immediate attention. Our recommendation is: have a licensed HVAC contractor evaluate further and repair or replace as needed.

6. Water Damage and Mold

Georgia's high humidity and heavy rainfall create ideal conditions for water intrusion and mold growth. Water damage is one of the most common and costly findings in Metro Atlanta home inspections.

Evidence of water damage includes:

  • Water stains on ceilings, walls, and around windows
  • Warped, buckled, or cupping hardwood floors
  • Visible mold growth on walls, ceilings, or in crawlspaces and attics
  • Musty odors indicating hidden mold behind walls or under flooring
  • Efflorescence (white mineral deposits) on basement or crawlspace walls

What this could mean: Active mold can cause respiratory health issues and indicates ongoing moisture problems that must be resolved. Professional mold remediation costs $5,000 to $15,000 depending on the extent of contamination. Our recommendation is: identify and correct the water source first, then have a licensed mold remediation company evaluate further and treat as needed. Read our crawlspace moisture guide for Georgia-specific prevention tips.

7. Pest and Termite Damage

The Southeast is one of the heaviest termite zones in the United States. Georgia's warm climate and abundant moisture make every home a potential target for subterranean termites, Formosan termites, carpenter ants, and wood-boring beetles.

Signs of pest damage include:

  • Mud shelter tubes running along foundation walls and piers
  • Hollow-sounding wood when tapped with a probe
  • Discarded termite wings near windows and doors
  • Active wood rot and fungal decay in crawlspaces and sill plates
  • Sawdust-like frass from wood-boring beetles

What this could mean: Extensive termite damage to structural framing can cost $10,000 to $25,000 to repair. Most homeowner insurance policies do not cover termite damage. Our recommendation is: add a dedicated WDO/termite inspection to obtain the Official Georgia Wood Infestation Report required for closing, and have a licensed pest control company evaluate further and treat as needed.

8. Structural Concerns

Beyond foundation-specific issues, inspectors evaluate the overall structural integrity of the home, including the framing, load-bearing walls, support beams, and connections between the roof and walls.

Structural red flags include:

  • Sagging ridge lines or rafters visible from the exterior
  • Cut or notched structural members where plumbers or HVAC installers have compromised load-bearing framing
  • Improperly supported beams or columns in basements and crawlspaces
  • Bowing or leaning walls
  • Deteriorated or absent hurricane ties and structural connectors

What this could mean: Structural deficiencies can affect the safety of the entire home and may violate building codes. Repairs range from $2,000 for supplemental supports to $20,000 or more for major structural remediation. Our recommendation is: have a licensed structural engineer evaluate further and design a repair plan.

9. Fire and Safety Code Violations

Safety code violations are especially significant because they present immediate danger to the occupants. While a home inspection is not a code compliance audit, experienced inspectors identify safety hazards that may violate current standards.

Common safety violations in Georgia homes:

  • Missing or non-functional smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms
  • Bedrooms without proper emergency egress windows
  • Stairs and decks missing required guardrails or with improper baluster spacing
  • Improperly vented gas appliances (water heaters, furnaces) creating carbon monoxide risks
  • Missing fire-rated separation between the garage and living space
  • Anti-tip brackets missing from freestanding ranges

What this could mean: Fire and safety violations put lives at risk. Most of these items are relatively inexpensive to correct (ranging from $50 to $1,000 each), but they must be addressed. Our recommendation is: correct all safety hazards before occupying the property.

10. Environmental Hazards

Environmental hazards include substances that pose long-term health risks to occupants. These are particularly important in Georgia homes built before 1980.

Environmental concerns include:

  • Radon gas: An invisible, odorless radioactive gas that is the second leading cause of lung cancer. Elevated levels have been found in homes across Fulton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Cobb, and Cherokee counties. Read our radon guide for Georgia.
  • Asbestos-containing materials: Found in older homes in floor tiles, pipe insulation, popcorn ceilings, and siding. Disturbing these materials releases dangerous fibers.
  • Lead-based paint: Present in homes built before 1978. Particularly dangerous for young children.

What this could mean: Environmental hazards require specialized testing and professional remediation. Radon mitigation systems cost $800 to $2,500 and are highly effective. Asbestos and lead paint abatement costs vary widely depending on scope. Our recommendation is: have the appropriate licensed environmental contractor evaluate further and remediate as needed.

What to Do If Issues Are Found

Discovering major defects during a home inspection can feel overwhelming, but it does not necessarily mean you should walk away from the property. Here is how experienced buyers handle inspection findings:

  1. Prioritize safety hazards and major defects. Focus on items that affect structural integrity, safety, and major systems (roof, HVAC, electrical, plumbing, foundation). Minor cosmetic issues are normal maintenance.
  2. Get contractor estimates. For major findings, obtain quotes from licensed contractors to understand the actual repair costs. This gives you factual data for negotiations.
  3. Negotiate with the seller. You can request that the seller make repairs before closing, offer a closing credit, or reduce the purchase price to account for needed work.
  4. Know when to walk away. If the seller refuses to address serious safety or structural concerns, or if the total repair costs exceed your budget and risk tolerance, exercising your inspection contingency is the smart decision.

For a detailed breakdown of how to interpret your inspection report, read our guide on understanding red flags vs. maintenance items.

Georgia-Specific Inspection Concerns

Metro Atlanta has several unique factors that affect home inspections:

  • Red clay soil: Georgia's expansive clay creates significant foundation stress through seasonal swelling and shrinking cycles.
  • High humidity: Crawlspace moisture, attic condensation, and mold are exceptionally common in our humid subtropical climate.
  • Termite pressure: Georgia is in one of the highest termite activity zones in the country. A WDO inspection is essential for every transaction.
  • Severe storm exposure: Summer thunderstorms, occasional hail, and high winds demand close attention to roof condition and exterior drainage.
  • Older neighborhoods: Many established Atlanta neighborhoods feature homes built in the 1950s through 1970s with outdated electrical, plumbing, and insulation systems.

The Foresight Advantage: Two Inspectors, Zero Guesswork

At Foresight Home Inspections, we send two certified inspectors on every single job. While one inspector focuses on the exterior systems, roofing, and grading, the other audits the interior systems, electrical panel, plumbing, and HVAC. This dual-inspector approach, combined with FLIR thermal imaging and our $10,000 Elite Master Inspection Warranty, ensures that every potential deal breaker is identified before you reach the closing table.

Ready to protect your investment? Use our Instant Quote Calculator to get your transparent price, or chat with Foresight AI to get expert answers 24/7. You can also call us directly at 678-480-2110 or visit our services page to explore all inspection options.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can a home actually fail an inspection?
A: Technically, no. A home inspection is not a pass-or-fail test. It is a detailed evaluation of the property's condition. However, major defects such as foundation failure, hazardous wiring, active roof leaks, or environmental dangers can effectively act as deal breakers that cause buyers to renegotiate or walk away from the transaction.

Q: What are the most expensive home inspection findings?
A: The most costly findings are typically foundation repairs ($5,000 to $30,000), roof replacement ($8,000 to $25,000), HVAC system replacement ($6,000 to $15,000), whole-house electrical rewiring ($8,000 to $15,000), and sewer line replacement ($5,000 to $15,000). These are the items that most frequently trigger renegotiations or deal cancellations.

Q: Should I walk away from a home with inspection issues?
A: Not necessarily. Most defects can be repaired. The key factors are: the total cost of repairs versus your budget, whether the seller is willing to negotiate, and whether the defects involve safety hazards you are not comfortable accepting. Your Foresight inspection report gives you the information you need to make a confident, informed decision.

Q: How long does a home inspection take in Georgia?
A: A comprehensive Foresight two-inspector home inspection typically takes 2 to 3 hours for a standard-sized home. Larger properties or inspections with multiple add-on services may take 3 to 4 hours. Your detailed report with photos is delivered within 24 hours.

Q: Are home inspection findings common in new construction homes?

Municipal code inspectors check minimum compliance, not quality. Read our new construction inspection guide for details on why every new home needs an independent inspection.

title: First-Time Home Buyer Inspection Checklist for Atlanta [2026]
description: The complete first-time home buyer inspection checklist for Atlanta in 2026. Organized by category with expert tips from Certified Master Inspector Christopher Boykin on what to expect, what to ask, and Georgia-specific items to watch for.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
keywords: what to look for in a home inspection
home inspection tips first time buyers
content:
Key Takeaway: As a first-time home buyer in Metro Atlanta, your home inspection is the single most important step to protect your investment. This comprehensive checklist covers every major category — exterior, interior, major systems, and safety — plus Georgia-specific concerns, questions to ask your inspector, and what to expect on inspection day.

Congratulations! If you are reading this, you are likely preparing to purchase your first home in the Metro Atlanta area. Buying a home is one of the most exciting and significant financial decisions you will ever make, and the home inspection is your best opportunity to understand exactly what you are buying before you commit.

As a first-time buyer, the home inspection process can feel overwhelming. What should you focus on? What questions should you ask? What are the most critical items specific to Georgia homes? In this comprehensive guide, Certified Master Inspector Christopher Boykin provides the complete home inspection checklist organized by category, along with expert tips to help you navigate the process with confidence.

What to Expect During Your Home Inspection

Before diving into the checklist, it is important to understand how the inspection process works:

  • Duration: A thorough home inspection for a standard-sized home (1,500 to 3,000 sq ft) typically takes 2 to 3 hours. At Foresight Home Inspections, our two-inspector team can be more efficient, but we never rush the process.
  • Your presence: You are strongly encouraged to attend your inspection. Walking through the home with your inspectors allows you to see findings firsthand, ask questions in real time, and learn about the home's systems and maintenance needs.
  • The report: After the inspection, you will receive a comprehensive digital report with high-resolution photos, detailed descriptions of every finding, and clear recommendations. Foresight delivers reports within 24 hours of the inspection.
  • What it is not: A home inspection is not a code compliance audit, an appraisal, or a guarantee that nothing will ever go wrong. It is a professional evaluation of the home's current condition based on visible and accessible components.

Exterior Inspection Checklist

The exterior of the home is your first line of defense against Georgia's intense weather, including heavy rainfall, high humidity, summer heat, and occasional severe storms. Here is what a professional inspector evaluates:

Roof

  • Condition of shingles, tiles, or metal roofing material (looking for cracks, curling, missing pieces, or granule loss)
  • Flashing around chimneys, skylights, vents, and roof valleys
  • Condition of gutters, downspouts, and splash blocks
  • Soffit and fascia boards for rot, damage, or pest entry
  • Estimated remaining useful life of the roof covering
  • Proper attic ventilation (ridge vents, soffit vents, or powered ventilators)

Siding and Exterior Walls

  • Condition of siding material (brick, vinyl, fiber cement, stucco, or wood)
  • Cracks in brick mortar joints (especially stair-step patterns indicating settlement)
  • Gaps or separations around windows and doors
  • Condition of exterior paint, trim, and caulking
  • Evidence of moisture intrusion or wood rot at exterior walls

Grading and Drainage

  • Ground slope away from the foundation (minimum 6 inches of fall in the first 10 feet)
  • Downspout extensions directing water at least 4 to 6 feet from the foundation
  • Evidence of standing water, erosion, or ponding near the foundation
  • Condition of retaining walls, if present
  • Driveway and walkway condition (cracks, settling, trip hazards)

Decks, Porches, and Patios

  • Structural integrity of deck framing, posts, and ledger board connections
  • Guardrail height (minimum 36 inches for residential decks) and baluster spacing (maximum 4 inches)
  • Condition of decking material (rot, insect damage, loose boards)
  • Stair condition and handrail presence

Interior Inspection Checklist

The interior inspection covers the living spaces, structural components, and finishes throughout the home:

Walls, Ceilings, and Floors

  • Cracks in drywall (hairline cracks vs. structural movement cracks)
  • Water stains on ceilings indicating past or active roof or plumbing leaks
  • Floor levelness (checking for slopes that may indicate foundation issues)
  • Condition of flooring materials throughout the home
  • Proper operation of all interior doors (sticking doors can indicate structural shifting)

Windows and Doors

  • Proper operation (opening, closing, locking) of all windows and exterior doors
  • Fogging between dual-pane glass (indicating broken window seals)
  • Condition of weather stripping and caulking
  • Egress compliance for bedroom windows (required for emergency escape)

Kitchen

  • Operation of all built-in appliances (dishwasher, range, oven, microwave, disposal)
  • Condition of countertops, cabinets, and sink fixtures
  • Evidence of leaks under the sink
  • GFCI protection on all countertop outlets
  • Proper range hood ventilation (vented to exterior vs. recirculating)

Bathrooms

  • Functional operation of all toilets, sinks, and tub/shower fixtures
  • Water pressure and drain speed at each fixture
  • Condition of tile, grout, and caulking around tubs and showers
  • GFCI protection on all bathroom outlets
  • Exhaust fan presence and proper venting to the exterior (not into the attic)
  • Evidence of moisture damage around tub and shower surrounds

Attic

  • Insulation type, depth, and coverage
  • Evidence of roof leaks (water stains on decking or rafters)
  • Proper ventilation to prevent heat and moisture buildup
  • HVAC ductwork condition (connected, sealed, and insulated)
  • Evidence of pest activity (rodent droppings, nesting, insect damage)
  • Structural framing condition (rafters, trusses, collar ties)

Crawlspace or Basement

  • Moisture levels and evidence of water intrusion
  • Vapor barrier presence and condition (for crawlspaces)
  • Foundation wall and pier condition
  • Floor joist and sill plate condition (checking for rot, insect damage, or sagging)
  • Plumbing and HVAC lines running through the space
  • Evidence of mold, fungal growth, or standing water

Georgia crawlspaces deserve special attention due to our humid climate. Read our complete crawlspace moisture guide for detailed prevention strategies.

Major Systems Checklist

The major systems of the home are the most expensive components to repair or replace. These items deserve your closest attention during the inspection:

Electrical System

  • Main electrical panel brand, capacity, and condition
  • Breaker connections (checking for double-taps, corrosion, or overheating)
  • Grounding and bonding compliance
  • GFCI protection in kitchens, bathrooms, garages, exterior, and laundry areas
  • AFCI protection in bedrooms (required in homes built after 2008)
  • Representative outlet testing throughout the home
  • Smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm presence and function

Plumbing System

  • Supply pipe material (copper, PEX, CPVC, or galvanized steel)
  • Drain pipe material (PVC, ABS, cast iron, or clay)
  • Water heater age, condition, and safety features (TPR valve, proper venting)
  • Water pressure at multiple fixtures
  • Evidence of leaks at supply lines, drain connections, and fixtures
  • Main water shut-off valve location and operation
  • Hose bibb (exterior faucet) condition

HVAC System

  • Age and condition of the air conditioning condenser and air handler or furnace
  • Temperature differential across the cooling coil (should be 15 to 20 degrees)
  • Filter condition and accessibility
  • Ductwork condition and insulation in attic and crawlspace
  • Thermostat operation
  • Combustion gas venting for gas furnaces and water heaters
  • Condensate drain line routing and condition

Safety Checklist

Safety items protect you and your family from immediate hazards. These should be treated as non-negotiable, regardless of cost:

  • Smoke detectors in every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level of the home
  • Carbon monoxide detectors near sleeping areas and on every level (required for homes with gas appliances or attached garages)
  • Fire extinguisher accessibility (recommended in kitchen and garage)
  • Guardrails on all elevated walking surfaces, stairs, and decks
  • Anti-tip bracket on freestanding kitchen ranges
  • Proper water heater TPR (Temperature and Pressure Relief) valve with discharge pipe
  • Tempered or safety glass in hazardous locations (shower doors, low windows near doors)
  • Garage door auto-reverse function (safety sensors)
  • Handrails on all stairways with four or more risers

Georgia-Specific Items to Watch For

Metro Atlanta has unique conditions that create specific inspection concerns. Make sure these Georgia-specific items are addressed:

  • Termite and WDO inspection: Georgia is in one of the highest termite activity zones in the country. A dedicated WDO inspection with the Official Georgia Wood Infestation Report is required by most lenders and is essential for every buyer.
  • Crawlspace moisture: Georgia's humidity makes crawlspace moisture one of the most common and damaging issues. Ensure your inspector physically enters the crawlspace (not just looks from the access point) to check for standing water, vapor barrier condition, and wood rot.
  • Red clay soil and foundation stress: The expansion and contraction of Georgia's red clay creates ongoing foundation pressure. Pay close attention to any signs of settlement, including stair-step brick cracks and sticking doors. See our foundation inspection guide.
  • Radon testing: Multiple Georgia counties show elevated radon levels. Add radon testing to your inspection, especially for homes with basements or slab foundations.
  • Aging sewer lines: Many established Metro Atlanta neighborhoods have homes with 30 to 60-year-old clay or cast iron sewer lines that are prone to root intrusion and collapse. A sewer scope inspection is strongly recommended for any home older than 20 years.
  • Storm damage history: Georgia experiences severe thunderstorms, occasional hail, and high winds. Have your inspector carefully evaluate the roof for storm damage, especially if the home has an older roof covering.
  • Polybutylene (poly-b) piping: This defective plumbing material was widely installed in Georgia homes from the late 1970s through the mid-1990s. It is prone to sudden, catastrophic failure and should be identified and planned for replacement.

Questions to Ask Your Home Inspector

As a first-time buyer, do not be afraid to ask questions throughout the inspection. Here are the most important questions to ask:

  1. "What are the most significant findings so far?" — Ask this periodically during the inspection to prioritize your focus and understand which items are major concerns versus minor maintenance.
  2. "What is the estimated remaining useful life of the major systems?" — Understanding when the roof, HVAC, and water heater will need replacement helps you budget for future expenses.
  3. "Are there any safety hazards that need immediate attention?" — Safety items should be addressed before you move in, regardless of negotiation outcomes.
  4. "What maintenance should I plan for in the first year?" — A good inspector will help you create a maintenance priority list so you know what to address first after closing.
  5. "Do you recommend any additional testing or specialist evaluations?" — If the inspector notices potential issues that require specialized evaluation (foundation, mold, sewer), they will recommend follow-up inspections.
  6. "Is this finding a safety concern, a major defect, or routine maintenance?" — Understanding the severity of each finding helps you prioritize your negotiation requests.
  7. "How does this home compare to others you have inspected in this area?" — Experienced local inspectors can provide valuable context about how the home stacks up against comparable properties.

Tips for First-Time Home Buyers

After performing thousands of inspections across Metro Atlanta, here are Christopher Boykin's top tips for first-time buyers:

  • Never skip the inspection. Even in a competitive market, waiving your inspection contingency is extremely risky. The few hundred dollars you invest in an inspection can save you tens of thousands in unexpected repairs.
  • Attend the inspection in person. Photos and reports are helpful, but there is no substitute for walking the property with your inspectors and seeing conditions firsthand.
  • Focus on the big picture. Cosmetic issues like paint color, outdated fixtures, or minor scuffs are easily fixed. Focus your attention and negotiation energy on structural, safety, and major system findings.
  • Get a two-inspector team. A single inspector working alone for 3 hours is under enormous pressure to cover everything. Two inspectors deliver double the expertise and significantly reduce the chance of missed findings.
  • Budget for add-on services. Radon testing ($175 to $200), termite inspection ($100 to $175), and sewer scope ($425) are small investments that protect you from major hidden problems. View our complete services and pricing.
  • Read the full report carefully. Do not skim your inspection report. Read every finding, review every photo, and ask your inspector to clarify anything you do not understand. Our guide on understanding red flags vs. maintenance can help.
  • Do not panic. Every home has findings. The question is not whether there are issues, but whether the issues are manageable and within your budget. A good inspection report empowers you with knowledge, not fear.

title: Crawlspace Moisture: The Silent Threat to Georgia Foundations
description: Crawlspace moisture is a major risk in Metro Atlanta. Learn the signs of wood rot and foundation damage from Certified Master Inspector Christopher Boykin.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
content:
In Metro Atlanta and across Georgia, many homes are built over a crawlspace rather than a basement or slab. Crawlspaces are incredibly common, but they also host one of the most frequent findings we uncover during home inspections: crawlspace moisture. Because of our highly humid summers and clay soils, moisture in crawlspaces is a silent threat that can damage structural integrity and diminish indoor air quality.

At Foresight Home Inspections, we send two certified inspectors on every single property audit. One of our primary tasks is to crawl directly into these tight spaces, equipped with FLIR thermal imaging cameras and digital moisture meters, to see what is happening beneath your feet. We don't just stand at the access door—we scan every corner of the floor framing to make sure your home is fully protected.

Why Crawlspace Moisture is a Major Risk in Georgia

Crawlspaces naturally accumulate humidity because they are situated directly over the bare soil. In North Georgia, heavy summer rains soak the clay around foundations, and this moisture slowly evaporates into the crawlspace air. When that warm, damp air contacts cooler floor joists or AC ducts, it condenses into water droplets.

If wood joists are exposed to this water for long periods, they begin to decay. Over time, this leads to structural sagging, spongy floors, and the growth of active mold spores. What this could mean is that your subfloor is rotting, your family is breathing mold spores through floor vents, or your foundation structure is losing its load-bearing capacity. Our recommendation in these situations is: have a licensed structural or moisture mitigation contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

Common Signs of a Wet Crawlspace You Can Spot

While you might not want to crawl under your house yourself, there are several warning signs you can easily spot from inside your living spaces:

  • Musty Odors — A persistent, damp smell in the home, particularly near baseboards and closets, is a classic sign of crawlspace mold.
  • Cupping Wood Floors — When crawlspace humidity is high, the bottom of hardwood flooring absorbs moisture and expands, causing the edges of the boards to cup or warp upward.
  • Sagging or Soft Spots — If walking across your living room feels slightly bouncy or uneven, the floor framing below may have lost strength due to rot.
  • High Indoor Humidity — Up to 50% of the air on the first floor of a home originates in the crawlspace due to the "stack effect." A wet crawlspace directly raises humidity throughout the house.

How to Solve Crawlspace Moisture Concerns

Fixing crawlspace moisture depends on how severe the water intrusion is. For minor humidity, installing a thick 6-mil or 10-mil vapor barrier over the bare soil is highly effective. The plastic barrier blocks ground moisture from rising into the air and keeps floor joists dry.

For more active leaks, a combination of a sump pump, perimeter french drains, or a crawlspace dehumidifier might be required. In extreme cases, full crawlspace encapsulation—where the space is completely sealed, insulated, and conditioned—is the gold standard. If we find excessive standing water or falling insulation under your house, our recommendation is: have a licensed crawlspace encapsulation contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

Every inspection we perform is also backed by our elite $10,000 Peace of Mind Protection Warranty at no additional cost, covering your structural wood framing and major systems for 90 days after closing.

Builders work under tight deadlines with multiple subcontractors, which frequently leads to skipped steps, improper mechanical installations, and structural errors. There is a common misconception among homebuyers in the Metro Atlanta area that buying a brand-new home means buying a perfect home. After all, the appliances are shiny, the paint is fresh, and the property has passed various city or county municipal inspections. However, as Certified Master Inspectors, we can tell you with absolute certainty: new construction homes are rarely perfect.

In the rapid-pace Atlanta real estate market, homebuilders coordinate dozens of different subcontractors working on multiple projects simultaneously. Under intense pressure to hit closing deadlines, quality control can easily slip. That is why understanding why new construction inspections are important is the single most valuable step you can take to safeguard your investment before signing the final papers.

Municipal Code Inspections vs. Private Master Inspections

Many buyers ask us, "Doesn't the city or county inspect the home during construction?" Yes, they do—but there is a massive difference in scope, time, and intent between a municipal code inspector and a private inspector from Foresight Home Inspections, LLC.

  • Time Constraints: Municipal inspectors are often overloaded, spending as little as 10 to 15 minutes per home. A private two person inspection team team from Foresight spends 2 to 3 hours thoroughly auditing every square inch of the property.
  • Minimum Code vs. Quality: County inspectors check only if the home meets the absolute minimum safety codes. They do not check for workmanship quality, manufacturing defects in equipment, cosmetic compliance, or systemic issues like improper roof flashing and ductwork layout.
  • Unbiased Buyer Representation: Municipal inspectors work for the local government. Our inspectors work exclusively for you, the buyer, with no conflict of interest. We evaluate the home from your perspective, ensuring you don't inherit hidden defects.

Common Defects Found in Brand-New Atlanta Homes

Even in high-end developments in Alpharetta, Marietta, or Decatur, we routinely uncover serious defects during new construction inspections. Some of the most common findings include:

  • Improper HVAC Duct Installation: Subcontractors often leave attic ducts completely disconnected, crushed, or unsealed. This causes your heating and air conditioning to blow directly into the attic, driving up utility bills and causing system strain.
  • Structural Framing and Roof Truss Modifications: Plumbers and HVAC installers sometimes cut through load-bearing studs or roof trusses to run pipes and ducts, severely compromising the structural integrity of the home.
  • Incomplete Exterior Grading: Proper soil grading is crucial to ensure rainwater runs away from the foundation. Builders frequently fail to grade the yard properly, leading to water pooling against foundation walls and basement walls within the first few rainstorms.
  • Electrical Hazards: Outlets are often wired in reverse polarity, GFCI protection is missing in wet areas, and breaker panels may have loose connections that present fire hazards.
  • Missing Insulation: Attics, crawlspaces, and exterior walls regularly have large gaps in insulation coverage, leading to hot/cold spots and high energy consumption.

What this could mean is that closing on the home without correcting these issues will leave you responsible for costly repairs down the line, once the builder's initial warranty expires. Our recommendation is: present our detailed digital report to the builder to have these defects corrected before closing.

The 3-Phase Inspection Approach

To ensure absolute protection, we recommend a phased inspection process during the build:

  1. Phase 1: Pre-Pour Slab/Foundation Inspection — Conducted before the concrete slab is poured, verifying that footings, vapor barriers, plumbing lines, and reinforcing steel are correctly positioned.
  2. Phase 2: Pre-Drywall / Framing Rough-In — Performed after the framing, plumbing, electrical, and HVAC lines are run, but before the drywall is installed. This is the only time we can inspect the home's "skeleton" to verify framing quality and line routing.
  3. Phase 3: Final Inspection Inspection — The final physical inspection of the completed home, testing all appliances, mechanicals, plumbing, roofing, and finished systems.

Common Signs of Foundation Issues in Georgia Homes

Foundation problems rarely happen overnight. They usually start with subtle warning signs that homeowners might overlook. If you notice any of the following indicators, it's time to schedule a professional assessment:

  • Sticking Doors or Windows — When the foundation shifts, door and window frames warp out of square, making doors difficult to open or close.
  • Sloping or Uneven Floors — A floor that slopes towards one side of the house often indicates settling joists or foundation walls.
  • Cracked Drywall or Brickwork — Horizontal or diagonal cracks above window frames, in drywall joints, or along exterior brick mortar lines (stair-step cracks) are classic settlement indicators.
  • Gaps Around Trim — Crown molding, baseboards, or cabinets separating from walls or ceilings suggest structural movement.

What this could mean is that your home is undergoing active foundation settlement, or there is localized soil erosion due to improper drainage. Our standard recommendation is: have a licensed foundation repair contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

What a Professional Foundation Inspection Covers

When our team performs an inspection, we look at the entire home's structural ecosystem, including:

  • Exterior Grading and Drainage — Water is the primary enemy of foundations. We evaluate the slope of the ground, gutter downspouts, and perimeter drainage to ensure water flows away from your foundation walls.
  • Crawlspace and Basement Inspection — We crawl under the home to examine foundation piers, floor joists, sills, and subflooring for bowing, cracking, wood rot, or active moisture intrusion.
  • Thermal Camera Scanning — Using FLIR thermal imaging, we detect temperature variations in foundation walls that reveal hidden water leaks, moisture pooling, or insulation gaps.
  • Framing and Support Posts — We verify that structural posts, beams, and columns are plumb, secure, and properly supported by adequate concrete footings.

Our two person inspection team team works meticulously to examine all the major systems of the home, ensuring you have a clear picture before you sign the closing papers.

The Core Structural Components and Foundation

First and foremost, a home inspector looks at the bones of the house. We check the foundation, walls, floor structure, and roof framing for any signs of movement, settling, or structural failure. In North Georgia, our heavy red clay soils can shift over time, which sometimes causes stress to foundations.

We look for cracks in foundation walls, sticking doors, uneven floors, or gaps around window frames. If we observe a hairline crack in a basement wall, we will describe the observation clearly. What this could mean is that minor settling has occurred, but it could also indicate active hydrostatic pressure or water intrusion issues. The Roofing, Attics, and Ventilation Systems

A failing roof can lead to catastrophic water damage throughout the entire home. We evaluate the roof covering, flashings, gutters, and downspouts. We also inspect the roof's ventilation, which is crucial for preventing heat and humidity buildup in Georgia's hot summers.

Inside the attic, we check the structure's framing, insulation levels, and ventilation pathways. If we find water stains on the roof decking or missing attic insulation, we document it with thermal imaging. What this could mean is that there is an active roof leak or that your energy bills will be higher than expected. We will recommend that you have a licensed roofing contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

Electrical Panels, Wiring, and Safety Hazards

Electrical safety is one of our highest priorities during any home inspection. We open the main electrical panel to check the wiring, breakers, and grounding. We also test a representative number of outlets and switches throughout the home, checking for proper wiring and GFCI protection in kitchens and bathrooms.

Common issues we find include double-tapped breakers, ungrounded outlets, or outdated wiring systems. If we identify an overloaded breaker panel or improper DIY wiring, we will flag it immediately. What this could mean is an elevated risk of electrical shock or house fires. We will advise you to have a licensed electrical contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

HVAC Systems and Plumbing Integrity

Georgia summers demand an efficient and fully functional air conditioning system. We test both the heating and cooling systems to verify they are operating within normal manufacturer specifications. We measure the temperature drop across the cooling coils to ensure the system is cooling properly.

We also inspect the plumbing system, including the water heater, supply lines, drain lines, and all fixtures. We check for leaks, low water pressure, and outdated materials. If we find a water heater with a rusted tank or active corrosion, we will document it. What this could mean is that the unit is nearing the end of its useful life and could leak catastrophically. We will suggest that you have a licensed plumbing contractor evaluate further and repair as needed.

title: The Hidden Dangers of Radon Gas in Georgia Homes
description: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer and can affect any home. Learn why radon testing should be part of every home inspection in Georgia.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
content:
Radon is an invisible, odorless radioactive gas that seeps into homes through cracks in the foundation, gaps around pipes, and openings in the slab. According to the EPA, radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer in the United States, responsible for an estimated 21,000 deaths annually. And it can be present in any home — new or old, well-sealed or drafty.

Why Georgia Homes Are at Risk

While Georgia isn't typically considered a "high radon" state like some northern regions, the EPA has identified elevated radon levels in homes across multiple Georgia counties, including Fulton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Cobb, Cherokee, and Forsyth. The red clay soils and granite bedrock common throughout North Georgia can produce radon that accumulates in enclosed spaces like basements and ground-level rooms.

How Professional Radon Testing Works

At Foresight Home Inspections, we use continuous 48-hour professional diagnostic monitors — not passive mail-in kits. Our equipment takes readings every hour, producing a detailed graph that shows exactly how radon levels fluctuate throughout the testing period. This gives you a far more accurate picture than a single-point test.

The EPA action level is 4.0 pCi/L (picocuries per liter). If your home tests above this threshold, a qualified radon mitigation contractor can install a sub-slab depressurization system that typically reduces levels by 90% or more.

When Should You Test?

The answer is simple: every time you buy a home. Even if a previous test showed low levels, radon concentrations can change over time due to shifts in the soil, changes in HVAC operation, or foundation settling. Testing costs just $200 as an add-on to any Foresight inspection — a small price for peace of mind about your family's long-term health.

title: The 11-Month Warranty Inspection: Your Last Chance to Catch Builder Mistakes
description: Your builder's warranty expires at 12 months. An 11-month warranty inspection is your final opportunity to identify defects covered under warranty. Here's what to know.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
content:
If you bought a newly built home, your builder almost certainly provided a one-year warranty covering defects in materials and workmanship. But here's the catch: once that 12-month window closes, you're on your own for any repairs. That's why the 11-month warranty inspection is one of the smartest investments a new homeowner can make.

Why Month 11?

By scheduling your inspection in the 11th month, you give yourself enough time to identify issues AND submit warranty claims before the deadline. Many problems don't surface immediately — they develop over the first year as the home goes through seasonal temperature changes, settling, and daily use.

What We Commonly Find at 11 Months

  • Drywall cracks and nail pops — Normal settling causes cosmetic cracks, especially around door frames and ceilings. These should be repaired under warranty.
  • Grout and caulk failures — Bathrooms and kitchens frequently show deteriorating caulk lines within the first year.
  • HVAC performance issues — Systems that worked fine in mild weather may struggle during Georgia's extreme summer heat. Temperature splits outside normal ranges indicate problems.
  • Window seal failures — Fogging between dual-pane glass indicates a broken seal that the builder should replace.
  • Drainage and grading changes — Soil settlement can redirect water toward the foundation instead of away from it.
  • Appliance issues — Dishwasher connections, garbage disposal mounting, and range hood venting problems that weren't apparent at move-in.

How It Works

Our two person inspection team team performs the same comprehensive inspection we do for any home purchase — covering structure, roof, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, insulation, and all major systems. After the inspection, you receive a detailed report with photos that serves as your official warranty claim punch list. Simply submit it to your builder and they're obligated to address covered items.

title: The Deep Dive: Why a Professional Pool & Spa Inspection is Critical
description: Buying a home with a swimming pool in Metro Atlanta? Discover why a specialized pool and spa inspection is necessary to avoid thousands in hidden plumbing, electrical, and structural repairs.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
content:
A swimming pool is the ultimate backyard escape—a sanctuary for hot Georgia summers, weekend barbecues, and family memories. However, for home buyers, a pool can also be a massive, water-filled liability. What looks like a sparkling, refreshing oasis during an open house can easily hide thousands of dollars in failing equipment, cracked structural shells, and dangerous electrical systems.

Many buyers mistakenly assume that a standard home inspection covers the swimming pool. In reality, a general home inspection strictly excludes pools and spas. Standard home inspectors are not certified to test chemical systems, mechanical pressure lines, automated controllers, or specialized underwater electrical components. That is why a dedicated Pool & Spa Inspection is an absolute necessity when buying a home with water features.

The Shocking Cons of Skipping a Pool Inspection

Pool repairs are among the most expensive home maintenance costs. Failing to inspect a pool before closing can lead to immediate financial strain:

  • Hidden Underground Plumbing Leaks: A pool's plumbing is buried deep beneath heavy concrete decks and soil. A slow leak in a return line or main drain can erode the surrounding soil, causing the pool shell or concrete deck to crack and sink. Repairing an underground pipe leak easily costs $5,000 to $10,000+ in excavation and restoration.
  • Lethal Electrical Hazards: Water and electricity are a deadly combination. Older pool lights, ungrounded pump motors, and faulty bonding grids present severe electrocution hazards that can turn a backyard swim into a tragedy. These hazards are completely invisible without professional diagnostic equipment.
  • Failing Mechanical Systems: Pool pumps, filters, automated control boards, and gas heaters have limited lifespans. Replacing a commercial-grade pool heater costs $3,500 to $5,000, while new variable-speed pumps run upwards of $1,800 to $2,500 installed.
  • Structural Shell Failures: Cracks in a concrete pool's structural gunite or plaster, tears in a vinyl liner, or blisters in a fiberglass shell are devastating. Vinyl liner replacement starts at $5,000, while resurfacing a gunite pool with modern pebble-tec plaster averages $8,000 to $15,000+.

The Pros of a Foresight Professional Pool & Spa Inspection

At Foresight Home Inspections, we perform detailed, non-invasive diagnostic evaluations of your pool and spa systems to protect your family and your wallet:

  • Full Structural and Mechanical Check: We inspect the coping, decking, plaster shell, and vinyl liners for structural defects. We run functional checks on all mechanical equipment, including pumps, filters, valves, heaters, and blowers.
  • Rigorous Safety and Compliance Audit: We evaluate critical child-safety boundaries, including self-closing gate locks, perimeter fencing heights, door alarms, and anti-entrapment drain covers complying with federal safety acts to keep your family completely safe and insurance-compliant.
  • Electrical Safety Inspection: We verify GFCI protection, inspect bonding wire systems, and check all electrical boxes and pool lights to eliminate electrocution risks.
  • Valuable Negotiation Leverage: Our clear, photographic report provides the precise recommendations and repair items you need. If we find a failing heater or structural crack, you can use the report to negotiate thousands off the purchase price or require the seller to perform the repairs prior to closing.

title: Under the Surface: The Ultimate Guide to Sewer Scope Inspections
description: Avoid a $10,000 excavation disaster. Learn why every home buyer in Georgia needs a high-definition sewer scope inspection to identify root intrusion, collapsed pipes, and hidden blockages.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
content:
When buying a home, it is easy to fall in love with what you can see: a modern kitchen, a spacious master bedroom, or a perfectly manicured lawn. But one of the most critical mechanical components of the home is completely buried underground, entirely out of sight. The main lateral sewer line runs from the house, under your yard, to the municipal main or septic tank. If this buried pipe is cracked, crushed, or clogged, it can lead to raw sewage backing up into your sinks, showers, and basement.

A standard home inspection only tests whether water drains out of the sinks at that moment. It cannot see the condition of the buried sewer pipe. A Sewer Scope Inspection uses a specialized, high-definition camera fed down the plumbing stack to examine the entire line, protecting you from a catastrophic plumbing disaster.

The Devastating Cons of Skipping a Sewer Scope

Sewer repairs are notoriously destructive and incredibly expensive. Here is what you risk by skipping a sewer scope scan:

  • Astronomical Repair Costs: Because sewer lines are buried deep underground, repairing them requires heavy excavation machinery, trenching through mature trees, and often tearing up concrete driveways or sidewalks. A typical sewer line replacement in Metro Atlanta costs between $5,000 and $15,000+.
  • Invasive Tree Root Destruction: Beautiful, mature trees are a hallmark of established Georgia neighborhoods. However, tree roots actively seek out moisture and nutrients. They will find the tiniest joints or micro-fractures in older clay or cast-iron sewer pipes, squeezing inside and expanding. This causes massive blockages and eventually shatters the pipes entirely.
  • Severe Structural and Health Hazards: A collapsed sewer line causes sewage to back up into the lowest level of the home. This introduces toxic bacteria, viral pathogens, and biohazards directly into your living space, ruining flooring, drywalls, and creating extensive mold growth.
  • Zero Insurance Coverage: Most standard homeowner's insurance policies explicitly exclude coverage for sewer backups or underground pipe collapses unless you have paid for a specialized, expensive rider. You will be entirely responsible for the bill.

The Pros of a Foresight Sewer Scope Inspection

Foresight Home Inspections uses state-of-the-art diagnostic equipment to inspect your sewer system thoroughly. Here is how we save you from financial ruin:

  • High-Definition Video Evidence: We run a self-leveling, high-resolution color camera through your lateral line, recording the entire journey. You get the actual video feed showing the precise internal condition of your pipes.
  • Precise Defect Localization: We spot cast-iron corrosion, clay pipe offsets, PVC cracks, pipe "bellies" (sagging areas where debris collects), and active root intrusions. We use digital transmitters to pinpoint the exact location and depth of any blockages, saving thousands in unnecessary excavation.
  • Pre-Closing Negotiation Power: Finding a sewer defect before closing is a massive win. You can present our professional video report to the seller and require them to replace the line, clear the tree roots, or provide a closing credit to cover the repairs. The $400 sewer scope fee regularly saves buyers over $10,000!

title: Termites & Wood Destroying Organisms: Protecting Your Home from Georgia's Silent Destroyers
description: Georgia's warm, humid climate makes it a haven for subterranean termites and wood-decay fungi. Learn why a WDO/termite inspection is crucial to safeguard your structure from catastrophic damage.
author: Christopher Boykin, CMI
content:
In the Southeast, termites are not a rare anomaly—they are an active, daily threat to residential properties. Georgia's warm, humid climate and abundant pine forests make it the perfect breeding ground for Eastern Subterranean Termites and aggressive Formosan Termites. Often referred to as "silent destroyers," termites chew through structural wood, support posts, and drywall paper 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, completely unnoticed behind walls until significant structural damage has already occurred.

A standard structural home inspection checks for visible signs of damage, but a dedicated Wood Destroying Organism (WDO) Inspection is required to thoroughly investigate for insect activity and secure the Official Georgia Wood Infestation Report needed for real estate closings.

The Catastrophic Cons of Skipping a WDO Inspection

Failing to verify active termites or pest damage before purchasing a home is a recipe for financial ruin. Here is why wood-destroying pests are so dangerous:

  • Compromised Structural Integrity: Termites feed directly on the structural framing, floor joists, subflooring, and wall studs of a home. Over time, this hollows out the lumber, causing floors to sag, walls to bow, and roofs to structurally fail. Rebuilding a termite-damaged home regularly costs $10,000 to $25,000+ in structural carpentry.
  • Absolutely Zero Insurance Coverage: Homeowner's insurance policies consider insect and termite damage to be "preventable maintenance" issues. Consequently, insurance will **never** cover the cost of termite remediation or structural repairs. If you buy a infested home, the entire remediation bill is yours to pay.
  • Lender and Financing Rejections: For many homebuyers utilizing VA, FHA, or conventional mortgage loans in Georgia, a clear WDO clearance is a strict regulatory requirement. Skipping this step or failing to secure a clean Official Georgia Wood Infestation Report can result in your mortgage underwriter immediately blocking your loan approval.

The Pros of a Foresight Termite & WDO Inspection

Foresight Home Inspections provides seamless WDO audits. Here is what we deliver:

  • Meticulous Physical Search: We inspect crawlspaces, basements, exterior foundations, sill plates, and attic spaces, actively checking for shelter mud tubes, wood damage, exit holes, and discarded wings.
  • Comprehensive Threat Audit: We don't just search for subterranean termites. We search for drywood termites, wood-boring powderpost beetles, carpenter ants, and active wood-rot decay fungi (which ruins more Georgia structures than all insects combined).
  • Conducive Condition Discovery: We identify and warn you about high-risk situations that invite termites, such as high soil lines covering exterior siding, crawlspace moisture issues, standing water, and direct wood-to-ground soil contact.
  • Official Georgia Infestation Report: We supply the standard, legally-compliant clearance letter required by your bank and closing attorney to guarantee a smooth, hassle-free closing.
